section.title: Deliver Me from My Enemies
section.sectionRationale: A Davidic lament composed when Saul sent armed men to watch David's house by night to kill him at daybreak, 1 Samuel 19:11-17, this psalm turns mortal danger into a pattern of praise, the enemies who prowl like snarling dogs are met by a psalmist resolved to sing of God's strength by morning.
section.thesis: Though enemies encircle his own house by night, David's urgent plea for deliverance turns, before the psalm ends, into resolved praise, for the God who is his fortress will expose the proud in His own time, a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who was likewise watched by hostile men yet prayed mercy over His enemies rather than their ruin.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the urgent plea for deliverance, verses 1-5, closing with Selah; the prowling enemies described as snarling dogs, contrasted with the psalmist's watchful trust, verses 6-10; the prayer that God expose and judge rather than instantly destroy, verses 11-13, closing with Selah; and the refrain of the prowling dogs answered at last by a resolved song of praise, verses 14-17.

verses.text: Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise against me.
Deliver me from workers of iniquity, and save me from men of bloodshed.
See how they lie in wait for me. Fierce men conspire against me for no transgression or sin of my own, O Lord.
For no fault of my own, they move swiftly to attack me. Arise to help me, and take notice.
O Lord God of Hosts, the God of Israel, rouse Yourself to punish all the nations; show no mercy to the wicked traitors. Selah

units.label: They return in the evening, snarling like dogs
units.note: the prowling enemies met by watchful trust

verses.text: They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city.
See what they spew from their mouths, sharp words from their lips: "For who can hear us?"
But You, O Lord, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations.
I will keep watch for You, O my strength, because You, O God, are my {{misgab|fortress}}.
My God of {{chesed|loving devotion}} will come to meet me; God will let me stare down my foes.

units.label: Consume them in wrath
units.note: a prayer for exposure and judgment, not silent vengeance

verses.text: Do not kill them, or my people will forget. Scatter them by Your power, and bring them down, O Lord, our shield.
By the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.
Consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, so it may be known to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob. Selah

units.label: But I will sing of Your strength
units.note: the refrain answered by resolved praise

verses.text: They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city.
They scavenge for food, and growl if they are not satisfied.
But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning. For You are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.
To You, O my strength, I sing praises, for You, O God, are my fortress, my God of loving devotion.

misgab.gloss: A high, secure stronghold set safely above the reach of the pursuer. David names God, not any physical refuge, his misgab three times in this psalm, framing the whole prayer as confidence in God's own unassailable protection rather than escape by his own cunning.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. Used three times in this psalm's closing movement, verses 10, 16, 17, it is the ground of David's confidence that the God who seems distant in the crisis will come to meet him and prove faithful.

basic.context: David wrote this psalm when Saul sent men to watch his house by night, meaning to kill him at daybreak, 1 Samuel 19:11-17. His wife Michal helped him escape through a window. The psalm moves from an urgent cry for rescue through a picture of enemies prowling like snarling dogs, to a resolve to sing of God's strength once morning comes.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm really was prayed on a specific, terrifying night, and it teaches that crisis prayer can end in praise before the danger itself has passed. David asks God not simply to kill his enemies but to expose them publicly, so that his people would remember and learn.
basic.originalLanguages: David calls God his misgab, fortress, a high place safe from the pursuer, and celebrates God's chesed, His steadfast, covenant loving devotion, in the very same breath as his fear. The one who feels hunted still knows himself loved.
basic.typology: The armed men who watch David's house to kill him foreshadow the hostile authorities who watched Jesus to find a charge against Him. And David's prayer that God expose rather than instantly destroy his enemies anticipates God's patient justice, fulfilled and transformed at the cross.
basic.christ: Jesus, like David, was watched by hostile men seeking His life, Mark 3:2. But where David prays God would scatter and expose his enemies, Jesus goes further, absorbing the assault Himself and praying, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, turning the psalm's cry for judgment into the gospel's offer of mercy.
basic.god: God is refuge and fortress for the hunted, sovereign judge of the nations who governs even surrounded by danger, and one whose settled, public justice, not frantic self-defense, will in the end expose every scheme of the wicked.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 19:11-17 supplies the historical crisis behind the psalm. Mark 3:2 shows Jesus similarly watched by hostile men. Luke 23:34 shows Jesus praying for the forgiveness of His executioners rather than their destruction.
basic.oneStory: David's night of hunted danger and his resolve to sing of God's strength by morning previews the pattern fulfilled in Christ, hunted by His enemies yet trusting His Father as fortress, whose mercy toward His killers opens the way for every enemy of God to become, through faith, one of His own.

context.literary:
Psalm 59 is built on two halves that mirror each other, and the mirror is the point. Each half opens with the enemies (verses 1 to 5 and 6 to 8 on one side, 11 to 15 on the other), and each half closes with the psalmist's answer, and the two answers are almost word for word the same: 'I will keep watch for You, O my strength, because You, O God, are my fortress' (verse 9) and 'To You, O my strength, I sing praises, for You, O God, are my fortress' (verse 17). Between them stands a refrain about the enemies, 'They return in the evening, snarling like dogs and prowling around the city' (verses 6 and 14). The enemy's refrain is repeated with a slightly different ending, from a hunt to a hunger, and the psalmist's refrain is repeated with a different verb, from watching to singing. The psalm moves from one to the other, from keeping watch to singing praise, and the change of verb is the whole story of a night that ends.

The time markers are carefully placed. Evening belongs to the enemies and morning belongs to the singer. They come back as the light goes (verse 6), and David says he will sing in the morning (verse 16). The psalm is an answer, in poetry, to the situation in which it was prayed.

The middle section is a daring request that is easy to misread. David asks God not to kill his enemies, because his people would forget, and in the next breath asks for them to be consumed until they are no more (verses 11 to 13). The two requests make sense only if the first is about how and the second is about what: he asks for judgment that is seen and remembered, and for an end to their power, and leaves the method to God. Two Selahs, at verses 5 and 13, mark the places where the singer is invited to stop and consider what has just been claimed about God as judge of the nations and ruler of Jacob.
context.historical:
The heading ties the psalm to a night Samuel describes: 'Then Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him and kill him in the morning' (1 Samuel 19:11). Saul's plan was to have the house watched through the night and strike at dawn, so that David was trapped inside his own home with the street full of men. Michal, who was Saul's daughter and David's wife, warned him to run that night, let him down through a window, and then placed a household idol in the bed with goat's hair at its head to make it look as though he lay sick (1 Samuel 19:12-16). The psalm puts into words what David felt between the moment he heard of the plot and the moment the window opened.

The city in which this happened, and the image of dogs, need a word of explanation. In the ancient Near East, dogs were mostly not household pets. They were scavengers that ran in packs through the streets at night, eating refuse and snarling over scraps. The picture in verses 6 and 14 is of men who come back every evening to the same streets, hungry, hunting the one person they have been sent to find. Verse 15 adds that they scavenge for food and growl when they are not satisfied, so that the same image turns from menace to a kind of pitiful restlessness.

The psalm uses the broader language of nations and of Jacob in verses 5, 8 and 13, which is part of why some readers think it was later sung in wider settings than David's night. Israel's worship kept the psalm and used it in ways that looked past a single house. Saul's men were, from David's point of view, traitors (verse 5, 'wicked traitors') because they betrayed the covenant community by serving a king who was trying to kill an innocent servant. 'Who can hear us?' (verse 7) is the usual boast of people who plot in the dark, and Psalm 10:11 and Psalm 94:7 show that it was an ancient temptation, to suppose that the God of Israel does not see.
context.canonical:
The same crisis gave rise to several psalms, and they are best read side by side. Psalm 57 is headed by a flight from Saul to a cave, and opens, 'Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes refuge. In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed' (Psalm 57:1). Both psalms use the image of hiding, and both resolve to sing in the morning. Psalm 59 is unusual in placing the danger at night and the joy at dawn, a pattern that runs through the Psalter: 'Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning' (Psalm 30:5), and 'Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning' (Psalm 143:8).

The images reappear in the Passion. 'Dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me' (Psalm 22:16) is another of David's prayers, and Christians have heard it fulfilled at the cross, where a circle of men stood watching a righteous man die. Jesus was also watched, by those who hoped to find a charge against Him (Mark 3:2), and He was arrested at night by men who had come out armed (Luke 22:52-53).

The window story gets an echo in the New Testament. After he came to faith in Damascus, Paul was hunted by men who watched the city gates day and night in order to kill him, and his friends let him down in a basket through a window in the wall (Acts 9:23-25; 2 Corinthians 11:32-33). Rahab had done the same for the spies (Joshua 2:15). The pattern is that God's servants escape by the help of people willing to open a window.

The word 'dogs' becomes a label in the apostolic letters for those who oppose the gospel from within (Philippians 3:2), and Revelation 22:15 pictures the dogs outside the city. The psalm's prayer that God be known 'to the ends of the earth' (verse 13) is taken up in the great commission and in the final scene in which every nation worships (Revelation 7:9).

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted the people of God to know how a believer prays in the dark. The psalm does not skip the fear. It gives the night its full weight: men lying in wait, men conspiring, men snarling in the street, and a man who has done nothing to deserve it (verses 3 and 4). He tells the truth about the danger and tells it to God.

He also meant to teach that the danger is not the last thing in the psalm. The psalm moves in a planned way from plea to confidence to praise, and the refrains make sure hearers feel the movement. By the last verses David has not yet been rescued, and he sings anyway. The morning that verse 16 promises is faith in God's strength, present before the evidence is.

And he meant his prayer for the enemies to teach something about God's justice and about the people He has chosen. The request that God not simply kill them but scatter and humble them, so that Israel would not forget (verse 11), shows that David thought of his own ordeal as a lesson for the nation. The plots of the wicked are to be exposed by their own words (verse 12), and the purpose is that 'it may be known to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob' (verse 13). Israel was meant to come away from the psalm convinced that their God sees what is done in the dark, however safe the plotters imagine they are.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David prayed on one night and what the threat was. It does not require believers to expect the same events or to pray in exactly the same terms. Nothing in it says that every hunted believer will be rescued through a window, and nothing in it says that the enemies should be hated as persons.

The pattern it offers is about how to pray under threat. Bring the situation to God by name and in detail. Say that you are innocent of the charge where you truly are, as David does, but do not claim more than that. Ask for rescue, and ask that God be seen as God. Decide what you will do when the morning comes, before it comes: 'I will sing of Your strength' (verse 16). This pattern is wise for Christians facing opposition, sickness, or fear of any kind.

The harsher requests are descriptive of a setting and need to be read with the rest of the Bible. The psalm says 'Consume them in wrath' (verse 13), but the man who says it also asks God not to kill them, and the New Testament shows the same God praying through His Son for the forgiveness of those who put Him on the cross (Luke 23:34). Believers are told to bless those who persecute them (Romans 12:14) and to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21). The psalm is not a model for acting against anyone but a model for telling God how it feels and leaving the outcome to Him.

debates.question: Is the psalm about David's night in 1 Samuel 19, or a later prayer for the nation?

views.label: A prayer from David's night in his house
views.case: The heading says it was prayed when Saul sent men to watch the house in order to kill him. The night setting, the men prowling about the city and the evening and morning contrast all fit 1 Samuel 19:11. Nothing in the psalm contradicts the heading, and the psalm's personal voice sounds like an individual under personal threat.

views.label: A psalm that began there and was adapted for wider use
views.case: The language of 'all the nations' and of God ruling over Jacob (verses 5, 8, 13) sounds national, and the psalm appears in a collection used in worship. On this view the original prayer was kept and sung when Israel was under threat from foreign powers, which is why the wider language sits beside the personal.

views.label: A psalm with a deliberately double horizon
views.case: Others say David himself meant the personal and the national to overlap, because he was the anointed king and his survival was tied to Israel's future. To threaten David was to threaten the line through which God had promised to bless the nations (2 Samuel 7:16).

debates.bearing: The heading is best taken seriously, since it gives the psalm a real setting and a real night. The wider language does not cancel it. It shows how a prayer prayed in one house became a prayer for all of Israel and, in the end, a prayer in which Christ's people can join.

debates.question: What does David mean by asking God not to kill his enemies, and then to consume them (verses 11 and 13)?

views.label: A prayer for public, memorable judgment
views.case: 'Do not kill them, or my people will forget' (verse 11) asks for something lasting. A sudden death would be over quickly. A judgment that scatters and humbles them and exposes their own words (verse 12) would be remembered. 'Consume them' in verse 13 then asks that their power end, not that every individual be destroyed at once.

views.label: A prayer with two stages
views.case: First the enemies are scattered and brought down, so that the people see what happens to those who oppose God's anointed. Then, in the end, their opposition is wiped out altogether. The psalm moves from a present hope to a final one.

views.label: A tension the psalm leaves open
views.case: Some readers say the two requests simply sit side by side. David is in fear and does not reason out every implication. The psalm is honest about a mind in crisis that asks for a number of things and leaves them with God.

debates.bearing: Whichever way it is read, the requests stay in God's hands, the purpose is that God's rule be known and not that the psalmist be gratified, and the psalm prepares for the New Testament's insistence that the enemy of the righteous is to be prayed for as well as judged (Matthew 5:44).

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm is full of words of protection and of attack, and the Hebrew gives them a particular colour. In verse 1 David asks to be protected from those who 'rise against' him. The verb at the root of 'protect', sagab, means to set on a height out of reach, and it is the cousin of the noun misgab, 'fortress', used in verses 9, 16 and 17. A misgab is a high place that the pursuer cannot climb. The request in verse 1 and the confession in verse 9 are therefore one thought at two moments, asking to be put on a height and saying that God is the height.

Verse 3 says the enemies 'lie in wait', and the verb is used of an ambush, as in Psalm 10:9 of a lion in his lair. David adds that they do so without his 'transgression or sin', two words, pesha and chatta'ah, that cover rebellion and missing the mark. He claims to be innocent of that charge, in the manner of 1 Samuel 24:11, and he makes the claim as a statement of fact about the charge, not as a claim to be sinless before God.

Verse 5 piles up divine titles: 'O Lord God of Hosts, the God of Israel'. The long form is what a person uses when he wants to appeal to everything God is. 'Hosts', tseva'ot, are the armies of heaven, and David names them on a night when he has no army. The 'wicked traitors' are literally those who act treacherously with iniquity, so the charge is one of betrayal.

In verse 9 the Hebrew text as it stands reads 'his strength', while verse 17 has 'my strength', and many take the first as a slip or variant for the second; the BSB follows verse 17. The matter affects the wording and not the sense. The word for strength, oz, is one that Israel used of God as their power, as in the song after the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:2).

Verse 10 has the phrase 'God of my loving devotion', literally the God of my chesed. The wording is possessive, so that the covenant love is his by promise. The verb 'meet' is qadam, which can mean to come before or to confront. Psalm 18:18 uses it of the enemies who 'confronted' David in the day of calamity, and here the same verb is used of God going out to meet David first. The hunters come to meet David; God comes to meet him ahead of them.

Verse 11 has the word 'shield', magen, which David uses of God in many psalms, and the verb 'forget', shakach, is the great danger of Israel's memory. Verse 16 shifts to 'sing', ranan, the word for a ringing cry of joy, and verse 17 to zamar, which is singing with instruments. The psalm ends on a full sound.

typology.type: David hunted in his own house, verses 1 to 4
typology.fulfillment: David, the anointed king waiting for his throne, is watched by armed men sent by the reigning king. The pattern is repeated with Jesus, the true Son of David, who was watched by those looking for a charge (Mark 3:2) and arrested at night by a crowd that came out with swords and clubs (Luke 22:52-53). In both cases the threat comes from those in authority over God's people. The escalation is that David was rescued out of the trap and Jesus walked into it, for the sake of those who were trapped by sin. The type falls short because David's escape preserved one man, while Christ's apparent defeat secured a people.

typology.type: The window and the morning, verses 9 and 16
typology.fulfillment: David escapes at night through a window and greets the morning with a song. The pattern of God bringing His servants out of the night and into the day is fulfilled in the resurrection, when the women come to the tomb at the first light of the week and find it empty (Luke 24:1-6). Psalm 30:5 says that weeping may stay the night but joy comes in the morning, and the resurrection is the morning the night was waiting for. The type falls short because David's morning was a reprieve and he later died, while Christ's morning is the beginning of a life that does not end (Romans 6:9).

typology.type: The fortress that is God Himself, verses 9, 16 and 17
typology.fulfillment: David calls God his fortress, a high place where the pursuer cannot reach. In the New Testament the refuge is found in a Person. Believers are told that their life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), and Christ Himself says that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand (John 10:28). Hebrews says that those who have taken refuge hold fast to the hope set before them, an anchor for the soul (Hebrews 6:18-19). The correspondence is that the fortress is no longer a place but a Saviour. The type falls short in that David's fortress protected his body for a season, while Christ secures the whole person for eternity.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by pattern. David's night in his house is the story of an anointed king who is hunted by those in power and kept by God. The man David prefigures was hunted in the same way. Herod looked for the infant Jesus to kill Him (Matthew 2:13), the leaders watched Him to find a charge (Mark 3:2), and on the night of His arrest men came with swords and clubs, and Jesus told them, 'this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness' (Luke 22:53). The night belonged to His enemies, as verse 6 has it.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the prayer. David asks that his enemies be scattered and exposed. Jesus, hunted by the same kind of men, did not call down legions of angels when He could have (Matthew 26:53), and He prayed for those who nailed Him up, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). The psalm's concern that God be known 'to the ends of the earth' is met in a way David could not have planned. The God who rules over Jacob is revealed in the cross as a God who takes the wrath upon Himself and offers forgiveness to His enemies, and Paul says that while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son (Romans 5:10).

It leads to Christ in the refrain about the morning. David's conviction that he will sing of God's strength 'in the morning' is fulfilled in a larger way on the first day of the week, when the night of the cross gives way to the empty tomb. The enemies who came back every evening had done what they could; by morning the tomb was open.

And it leads to Christ by the fortress. David calls God his misgab, his high place, and his refuge in times of trouble (verse 16). The New Testament says that the people of Christ are hidden with Him in God (Colossians 3:3), and that nothing in all creation can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38-39). Christ does not only point to a refuge; He becomes the place where the hunted can be safe.

A caution keeps this honest. David's specific details, the window, the household idol and the goat's hair, are not secret pictures of Christ. What the psalm supplies is a pattern of a righteous man hunted by those in power and kept by God, together with a real hope for the day when God's strength will be sung about. The New Testament's own uses of the psalm's images, and the life of Jesus, show where the pattern finds its fullest answer.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as a God who sees. David begins by asking Him to 'see how they lie in wait' (verse 3) and to 'see what they spew from their mouths' (verse 7), and the ground of his confidence is that the enemies' question, 'Who can hear us?', has a clear answer. The God of Israel hears what is said in the dark. Psalm 94:9 asks whether the one who formed the ear does not hear, and this psalm puts the question into a night on a street outside a house.

It shows God as a God who laughs. Verse 8 says that the Lord laughs at the enemies and scoffs at all the nations. The laugh is not cruelty. It is the recognition that plots against the Lord's anointed are smaller than they look. Psalm 2:4 says that the One enthroned in heaven laughs, and Psalm 37:13 that the Lord laughs because He sees that the wicked man's day is coming. It is meant to comfort the hunted, not to teach them to mock.

It shows God as faithful in love. David calls Him 'my God of loving devotion' and says that He 'will come to meet me' (verse 10). The psalm is full of power words, strength, fortress, shield, but the word it lingers on at the turning points is chesed, covenant love. The same God who is mighty enough to scatter the nations is tender enough to meet one frightened man at the door.

It shows God as the ruler of Jacob whose rule is meant to be known to the ends of the earth (verse 13). The psalm holds a tension that is typical of Scripture: God is at once the personal refuge of one man in one house and the ruler of the nations, whom the psalm asks to rouse Himself and punish the wicked traitors (verse 5). The same Lord who stands over all peoples is the one David addresses as 'my strength'.

For worship the psalm teaches that praise can be sung before rescue arrives. It is easy to praise God after the morning comes. David commits in advance: 'I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning' (verse 16). Faith like this does not wait for the situation to improve. It also teaches us to name God in terms that fit what we need, fortress, shield, strength, and to say them to Him in the very moment we need them. And it teaches that the God we sing to is the same in the night as in the morning, which is what makes the change of verbs between verses 9 and 17 possible.

crossReferences.note: The story behind the heading. Saul sends men to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, Michal warns him, lets him down through a window and puts a household idol in his bed. Reading it beside the psalm shows what the night felt like from inside the house.

A prayer from the same period of flight from Saul. David takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings until the danger has passed. It shares Psalm 59's pattern of fear turning to praise, and the two together show that David composed several prayers out of these years.

'Dogs surround me; a band of evil men encircles me.' The same picture of dogs as the men who hem in the righteous appears in another prayer of David, and the New Testament reads its details as fulfilled at the cross.
The One enthroned in heaven laughs and taunts the rebel kings. The laughter of Psalm 59:8 is the same laughter: the rebellion against God's anointed looks fearful from below and small from above.
'Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.' The same night-and-morning pattern as Psalm 59:16, expressed as a general truth of how God deals with His people.

'Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning... Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.' The two prayers share the pairing of morning, covenant love and rescue from enemies, and show how David's prayers feed one another.

Jesus is watched by people looking for a charge against Him. It is the same watching that David endured, from the same kind of people, and it shows that the Son of David is treated like the first David.

Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' Where David asks God to scatter his enemies, Jesus asks the Father to forgive His, and the prayer answers the psalm's wish that God's rule be known to the ends of the earth.

Paul is hunted by men who watch the gates day and night, and his friends let him down in a basket through a window in the wall. The story is a close echo of David's escape, and it shows the same God rescuing the later servants of the same gospel.

Believers' lives are hidden with Christ in God. It is the New Testament form of the psalm's fortress, in which refuge is found in a person and not in a place, and it makes David's confidence available to all who belong to Him.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that began in the garden. When the serpent turned humanity away from God, enmity was set between the serpent's offspring and the woman's (Genesis 3:15), and from then on the people of God have lived among hunters. Cain hunts Abel, Pharaoh hunts the Hebrew boys, and Saul hunts David. Each time the question is whether God sees and whether He will act. Psalm 59 belongs to the long line of answers that say He does, and that the proper response is to watch for Him.

It sets up what follows by giving Israel a template for their own dark nights. The psalm was kept in the collection, was sung after the night had passed, and was taken up by later generations who lived under foreign powers and again felt the streets full of men at dusk. When the exiles sat by the waters of Babylon and when the faithful of the second temple period lived under empires, David's night was a script they could use.

The story's centre is the night in Gethsemane and the morning of the empty tomb. The Son of David was hunted, watched, arrested in the dark and killed, and then raised at dawn. The psalm's movement from the evening of the dogs to the morning of the song is the shape of Good Friday and Easter. The rescue that David received through a window was given to the world through an open tomb, and Paul says that through this death Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15).

The church now lives between that morning and the final one. It is sometimes hunted, as Paul was, and it still watches for God and sings to Him before the final rescue. The prayer that God's rule be known to the ends of the earth is being answered as the gospel goes out to all the nations, and Revelation 7:9 pictures a great multitude from every nation standing before the throne.

It ends in the new creation. Revelation 22:3-5 promises that there will be no more night in the city, and that God's servants will see His face. The hunters who came back each evening have no place there, for outside are the dogs (Revelation 22:15), and inside the people of God will have nothing to watch for, because the one they waited for has come. The fortress of the psalm becomes a city with no need of walls against the dark.

quiz.q: What historical situation prompted this psalm, per its superscription?

options.text: When Saul sent men to watch David's house to kill him.
options.note: The superscription ties the psalm directly to 1 Samuel 19:11-17, when Saul's men surrounded David's house by night.

options.text: When the Philistines seized David in Gath.
options.note: That crisis lies behind Psalm 56, a different danger David faced.

options.text: When David fled from his son Absalom's rebellion.
options.note: That crisis lies behind Psalm 3, a later and different danger in David's life.

options.text: When David was crowned king over all Israel.
options.note: This was a moment of triumph, not the mortal danger this psalm describes.

quiz.q: What repeated image describes the enemies in verses 6 and 14?

options.text: Snarling like dogs, prowling around the city.
options.note: This refrain frames the psalm's central movements, picturing relentless, threatening hostility.

options.text: Roaring like lions in the wilderness.
options.note: A similar predator image, but not the one this psalm actually uses.

options.text: Circling like vultures overhead.
options.note: The psalm's image is dogs prowling the city, not birds circling.

options.text: Standing silently at the gates.
options.note: The enemies are described as loud and prowling, not silent.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do with his enemies in verse 11, rather than killing them at once?

options.text: Scatter them by Your power and bring them down, so that his people do not forget.
options.note: David wants God's justice publicly seen and remembered, not simply completed out of sight.

options.text: Convert them into allies overnight.
options.note: The psalm prays for judgment on the wicked, not reconciliation with them.

options.text: Kill them immediately and completely.
options.note: Verse 11 specifically asks God not to do this yet, so his people will remember.

options.text: Ignore them entirely and let them go free.
options.note: David is not indifferent to justice; he actively prays for God's judgment on them.

quiz.q: How does the psalm end, in verses 16-17?

options.text: With a resolved song of praise: 'I will sing of Your strength... for You are my fortress.'
options.note: The psalm moves from urgent fear to settled praise before the crisis has necessarily ended.

options.text: With a description of the enemies' final destruction.
options.note: Judgment is prayed for earlier, verses 11-13, but the psalm's actual close is praise, not a scene of destruction.

options.text: With a demand that God act immediately or David will give up.
options.note: The tone of the ending is settled trust and praise, not an ultimatum.

options.text: With continued despair and no resolution.
options.note: The psalm resolves into confident praise, not unresolved despair.

quiz.q: How does Jesus' response to His enemies deepen this psalm's prayer for justice?

options.text: Jesus prayed for the forgiveness of His executioners, offering mercy while still affirming God's coming judgment on the unrepentant.
options.note: Luke 23:34 shows Jesus extending mercy even as the New Testament affirms final judgment remains God's to give.

options.text: Jesus asked God to destroy His enemies immediately, exactly as David prayed.
options.note: Jesus instead prayed for their forgiveness, going beyond David's specific request.

options.text: Jesus fought back physically against those who arrested Him.
options.note: Jesus explicitly refused violent resistance, Matthew 26:52-53.

options.text: Jesus ignored His enemies completely and never addressed them.
options.note: Jesus directly addressed His executioners in prayer, Luke 23:34.

questions: David was watched by armed men in his own home yet resolved to sing of God's strength 'in the morning.' What situation are you facing right now where you need to trust God's protection through the night before you can sing in the morning?

The refrain 'they return in the evening, snarling like dogs' repeats in verses 6 and 14. What relentless pressure or fear keeps circling back in your life, and how does David turning that repetition into praise, rather than despair, speak to you?

David prays that God would expose and scatter his enemies rather than destroy them outright, 'or my people will forget,' verse 11. Where do you need patience for God's justice to be seen rather than demanding it happen instantly?

Jesus, watched by hostile men just as David was, prayed for His enemies rather than for their destruction. How does knowing Christ absorbed judgment for His enemies change how you pray for people who oppose you?
David calls God his fortress and His loving devotion in the same breath, verses 16-17. Where do you need both God's strength and His steadfast love this week?

translationNotes.note: Deliver renders a Hebrew verb for high, safe rescue; the same root idea reappears in the fortress imagery of verses 9, 16, and 17, unifying the psalm's plea and its praise.
Snarling like dogs pictures the roaming, scavenging street dogs of the ancient Near East, an image of restless, threatening hostility repeated at verse 14 to frame the psalm's movements.
Loving devotion renders chesed, God's covenant loyalty; David's confidence rests not in his own strength but in this steadfast character of God.
